quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Farmers often believe that more fertilizer means bigger harvests. Up to a point, this is true, since plants need nutrients to grow. Beyond that point, however, extra fertilizer adds little and can even reduce yields by damaging roots. The surplus is also washed into rivers, where it feeds algae that use up oxygen and harm fish. Precision farming techniques measure the soil and apply only what each part of a field requires. Farmers who use them often reduce costs while keeping yields stable. Agricultural advisers in several regions now offer free soil tests to help farmers decide how much fertilizer their fields actually need each season.
quests.question: Yields keep rising however much fertilizer is added.
quests.hint: What happens beyond a certain point?
quests.explanation: Extra fertilizer adds little and can even reduce yields.
quests.evidenceLine: Beyond that point, however, extra fertilizer adds little and can even reduce yields by damaging roots.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: A bank advertises a savings account with an interest rate of four percent, which sounds generous. Inflation, however, is running at five percent, so the purchasing power of the savings is shrinking. The advertisement does not mention the real interest rate, which is what matters to a saver. Some accounts also require the money to remain untouched for a year, and early withdrawal carries a penalty. Customers who compare accounts should therefore look at conditions as well as headline rates. Not all savers read the small print. Consumer organizations regularly publish tables that compare the real returns of different accounts, and they advise savers to update their comparisons every year.
quests.question: A saver in this account gains purchasing power each year.
quests.hint: Set the four percent against the five percent.
quests.explanation: Inflation of five percent exceeds the four percent interest, so purchasing power shrinks.
quests.evidenceLine: Inflation, however, is running at five percent, so the purchasing power of the savings is shrinking.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Hospitals learn from mistakes by reporting near misses, incidents that could have harmed a patient but did not. Staff are encouraged to report them without fear of punishment, because blame discourages honesty. Analysis of many reports reveals patterns, such as similar drug names being confused or unclear labels. Changes to packaging or procedures can then prevent real harm. Aviation adopted a similar approach decades earlier and credits it with a large fall in accidents. Hospitals hope to achieve comparable results. Several patient safety charities now run training courses for hospital staff that use anonymous examples from the reports to illustrate typical errors.
quests.question: Reporting near misses helps hospitals find patterns that they can fix.
quests.hint: Follow what analysis of many reports reveals.
quests.explanation: Patterns emerge from many reports, and changes to packaging or procedures can then prevent harm.
quests.evidenceLine: Analysis of many reports reveals patterns, such as similar drug names being confused or unclear labels. Changes to packaging or procedures can then prevent real harm.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Ants of some species farm fungus inside their nests, providing it with chopped leaves to feed on. The fungus, in turn, produces food that the ants cannot get directly from the leaves. Scientists believe that this partnership began tens of millions of years ago. The ants also protect their crop from diseases by producing antibiotics that are secreted by bacteria on their bodies. If the fungus is lost, the colony cannot survive. Young queens carry a piece of fungus with them when they leave to found new nests. Scientists studying these ants have found that different species farm different kinds of fungus, and each colony maintains its own carefully tended garden.
quests.question: A colony of these ants could not survive without its fungus.
quests.hint: Read what happens if the fungus is lost.
quests.explanation: The passage states that the colony cannot survive if the fungus is lost.
quests.evidenceLine: If the fungus is lost, the colony cannot survive.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Researchers wanted to know whether a new fertilizer improved crop growth. They divided a field into many plots, applied the fertilizer to half of them at random, and compared the harvests. Random assignment matters because it prevents the better soil or sunnier corners from being unintentionally given to one group. The fertilized plots produced about eight percent more. Yet the researchers cautioned that the result might not apply to different soils or climates. They recommended repeating the trial in other regions. Statisticians say that such trials are especially valuable in agriculture, where soil, weather, and sunlight can differ greatly even within a single small field.
quests.question: Random assignment helped the researchers avoid giving one group better conditions.
quests.hint: Why does random assignment matter?
quests.explanation: It prevents better soil or sunnier corners from going unintentionally to one group.
quests.evidenceLine: Random assignment matters because it prevents the better soil or sunnier corners from being unintentionally given to one group.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Many cities compete to become known as innovative, but the label is easier to claim than to measure. Officials often point to the number of start-up companies or the speed of the internet. Critics argue that these measures ignore whether ordinary residents benefit. A city might have shiny technology districts alongside crowded, unreliable public transport. Some researchers propose measuring the time residents spend traveling to work or waiting for services. Such measures are less glamorous but arguably more relevant. The debate is likely to continue, because different residents value different things, and no single ranking can satisfy everyone who lives or works in a city.
quests.question: Researchers propose that a city's innovation should be judged by its number of start-ups.
quests.hint: What do some researchers propose measuring instead?
quests.explanation: They propose measuring residents' travel and waiting times.
quests.evidenceLine: Some researchers propose measuring the time residents spend traveling to work or waiting for services.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Machine translation has improved so much that many people assume human translators will soon be unnecessary. For simple, factual text, the results are often good enough. Literary works, jokes, and legal contracts, however, contain subtle meanings that programs still handle poorly. A mistranslated clause in a contract can cost a company a great deal of money. Professional translators increasingly work by correcting machine output rather than starting from scratch. Their expertise remains essential where accuracy matters. Language technology companies acknowledge these limits and often advise customers to have important documents checked by a human reader before signing or sending them.
quests.question: Machine translation now handles legal contracts as reliably as skilled translators do.
quests.hint: Which kinds of text still cause difficulty?
quests.explanation: Literary works, jokes, and legal contracts contain subtle meanings that programs handle poorly.
quests.evidenceLine: Literary works, jokes, and legal contracts, however, contain subtle meanings that programs still handle poorly.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Historians who study the past rely on sources, but sources are never neutral. A royal chronicle, for example, was often written to praise the ruler and may omit defeats. A diary can be honest yet reflect only one person's limited view. Historians therefore compare sources against each other and ask who wrote them, why, and for whom. When accounts agree despite different motives, they can be trusted more. Disagreements are not failures but clues. Students of history are therefore taught early to read documents critically and to identify the position of the person who wrote them.
quests.question: Historians treat agreement between sources with different motives as a sign of reliability.
quests.hint: Read what happens when accounts agree despite different motives.
quests.explanation: Such accounts can be trusted more.
quests.evidenceLine: When accounts agree despite different motives, they can be trusted more.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Many people set New Year's resolutions and abandon them within weeks. Researchers suggest that this happens because resolutions are usually vague, ambitious, and dependent on motivation that fades. People are more successful when they choose one small change, link it to something they already do, and forgive occasional lapses. A single missed day rarely destroys a habit, but the belief that it has can. Progress is therefore a matter of resuming quickly. Perfection is not required. Coaches and psychologists who work with athletes often advise a similar approach, encouraging people to treat a lapse as information rather than as failure.
quests.question: Researchers say that one missed day usually ends a habit for good.
quests.hint: What effect does a single missed day rarely have?
quests.explanation: It rarely destroys a habit, though believing it has can.
quests.evidenceLine: A single missed day rarely destroys a habit, but the belief that it has can.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Rewilding projects reintroduce species that were once lost from an area, hoping to restore natural processes. When wolves returned to a large American park, elk changed their behavior and stopped grazing near rivers. Willows and other trees recovered along the banks, which stabilized the soil and provided habitat for birds and beavers. Scientists still debate how much of the change was due to the wolves and how much to other factors such as climate. The story remains popular because it shows how connected ecosystems are. Nevertheless, the exact size of the effect is uncertain. Wildlife managers in other countries are now considering similar projects, although they emphasize that each ecosystem has its own history and that results cannot simply be copied.
quests.question: Scientists remain unsure how much of the recovery was caused by the wolves.
quests.hint: What do scientists still debate?
quests.explanation: They debate how much of the change was due to the wolves.
quests.evidenceLine: Scientists still debate how much of the change was due to the wolves and how much to other factors such as climate.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Growing up, Mateo believed that his parents' quarrels meant that they did not love each other. Only as an adult did he understand that they argued about small things because they felt safe enough to be frank. His own marriage taught him that silence can be more dangerous than argument. He and his wife now try to raise problems early and in a calm tone. Their children sometimes roll their eyes at these conversations. Mateo hopes that they will learn from them. His daughter, now a teenager, says she is beginning to understand what he means, though she still prefers to avoid arguments at the dinner table.
quests.question: Mateo's opinion of his parents' arguments changed when he became an adult.
quests.hint: Compare what he believed as a child with what he understood later.
quests.explanation: As a child he thought quarrels meant no love, and as an adult he saw they reflected feeling safe.
quests.evidenceLine: Only as an adult did he understand that they argued about small things because they felt safe enough to be frank.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: A traveler who books the cheapest hotel in a popular city may be surprised by its location. Rooms far from the center can save money, but daily transport costs and lost time reduce the saving. A slightly more expensive hotel near the main sights may therefore be better value. Review websites can help, though ratings vary between sites and some reviews are unreliable. Comparing several sources is wise. Few travelers do it thoroughly. Many travel blogs suggest building a small budget for local transport before choosing a hotel so that the real total is clear in advance.
quests.question: Once transport is included, a distant hotel is guaranteed to cost less.
quests.hint: What reduces the saving from a distant room?
quests.explanation: Daily transport costs and lost time reduce it, so a lower cost is not guaranteed.
quests.evidenceLine: Rooms far from the center can save money, but daily transport costs and lost time reduce the saving. A slightly more expensive hotel near the main sights may therefore be better value.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Fact-checking organizations verify claims made by politicians and viral posts. They rate statements on a scale from true to false, explaining the evidence behind each rating. Critics say that the organizations are biased, since choosing which claims to check involves judgment. Defenders reply that transparency about methods and sources allows readers to judge for themselves. Studies suggest that corrections are more effective when they are clear, prompt, and come from a source the reader trusts. No system is perfect. Several social media companies have begun to work with such organizations, although their methods for labeling misleading posts remain a matter of active public debate.
quests.question: Fact-checkers explain the evidence behind each rating.
quests.hint: Read how the ratings are presented.
quests.explanation: They rate statements while explaining the evidence for each rating.
quests.evidenceLine: They rate statements on a scale from true to false, explaining the evidence behind each rating.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: In many societies, festivals mark the change of seasons, but the meanings attached to them shift over time. A harvest festival that once expressed gratitude for food may today be mainly a family gathering with little link to farming. Some communities deliberately revive older customs to strengthen local identity. Others let traditions change naturally as people move away and new members join. Scholars note that traditions often seem older than they are, since many were shaped in the last two centuries. Age alone does not make a custom authentic. Anthropologists who study festivals often find that the people who take part care less about the age of a tradition than about the feeling of belonging.
quests.question: Some communities revive old customs on purpose.
quests.hint: Which sentence starts with "Some communities"?
quests.explanation: The passage says some communities deliberately revive older customs.
quests.evidenceLine: Some communities deliberately revive older customs to strengthen local identity.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Architects designing a concert hall must think about sound as much as about appearance. Hard surfaces reflect sound, producing echoes, while soft materials absorb it and make music seem dull. The ideal balance depends on the kind of music: speech needs clarity, while orchestral music benefits from a longer, warmer resonance. Modern halls often include adjustable panels that change the acoustics for different performances. Even so, no hall is perfect for every kind of music. Musicians tend to have strong opinions about their favorites. The best-known halls, such as those built in the nineteenth century, are admired for their sound, though architects today rely on computer models as well as experience.
quests.question: Some modern concert halls can change their acoustics for different performances.
quests.hint: Look for the feature of modern halls.
quests.explanation: Adjustable panels change the acoustics for different performances.
quests.evidenceLine: Modern halls often include adjustable panels that change the acoustics for different performances.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Many people assume that keeping a house warm all day is cheaper than heating it only when needed. Engineers explain that a house loses heat faster the bigger the difference between inside and outside temperature. A cool house loses less heat, so switching the heating off while nobody is at home generally saves energy. The saving is smaller in poorly insulated buildings, which cool quickly and take a long time to reheat. Smart thermostats can learn a household's pattern and optimize the timing. Results vary from home to home. The energy agency advises households to make small adjustments and to monitor their bills for a few weeks before drawing conclusions about the results.
quests.question: Engineers say that keeping the heating on all day is the cheaper option.
quests.hint: What do engineers say about switching the heating off?
quests.explanation: It generally saves energy, since a cool house loses less heat.
quests.evidenceLine: A cool house loses less heat, so switching the heating off while nobody is at home generally saves energy.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: A city discovered that many of its parks were used mostly by a small number of regular visitors. A survey of residents who never visited them gave several reasons: they felt unsafe after dark, lacked seating, or found nothing suited to their age. The council added lighting, benches, and activities for teenagers and older adults. Within a year, the number of different visitors rose by a third. Officials concluded that quality of design mattered more than the size of the parks. Some neighbors still complain about the noise. The department now publishes a yearly report on how each park is used, and it invites residents to suggest further improvements online.
quests.question: The council's changes responded to what non-visitors had said.
quests.hint: Match the survey's reasons with the council's additions.
quests.explanation: Non-visitors cited safety, seating, and activities, and the council added lighting, benches, and activities.
quests.evidenceLine: A survey of residents who never visited them gave several reasons: they felt unsafe after dark, lacked seating, or found nothing suited to their age. The council added lighting, benches, and activities for teenagers and older adults.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Seeds of some desert plants remain dormant for years until enough rain falls. When a heavy shower finally arrives, the desert can turn green within days, as thousands of flowers open at once. The plants complete their life cycle quickly, producing new seeds before the soil dries again. Because the seeds respond only to substantial rainfall, they are not fooled by brief showers that would be too little to sustain them. Researchers believe that chemical inhibitors in the seed coat are washed away by enough water. The display may occur only once in several years. Botanists say that protecting these fragile habitats is important, since a single season of heavy grazing or trampling can damage seeds that took years to form.
quests.question: Brief showers do not trigger these seeds to grow.
quests.hint: What do the seeds respond to?
quests.explanation: Only substantial rainfall, so brief showers do not fool them.
quests.evidenceLine: Because the seeds respond only to substantial rainfall, they are not fooled by brief showers that would be too little to sustain them.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Many people think that a seat belt is unnecessary on short trips at low speeds. Yet a large share of serious injuries occur close to home, in journeys of a few kilometers. Even at moderate speed, a collision can throw an unrestrained passenger against the interior or out of the car. Passengers in the back seat also endanger those in front if they are not belted. Laws requiring rear seat belts have been introduced in many places for this reason. Most safety experts consider the matter settled. In several countries, television campaigns show the results of crash tests to remind people that the danger exists on every journey, whatever its length.
quests.question: Experts say seat belts are needed on long or fast journeys but not on short ones.
quests.hint: Where do many serious injuries occur?
quests.explanation: Close to home, on journeys of a few kilometers.
quests.evidenceLine: Yet a large share of serious injuries occur close to home, in journeys of a few kilometers. Even at moderate speed, a collision can throw an unrestrained passenger against the interior or out of the car.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Screening tests look for diseases in people who have no symptoms, and they can save lives. However, no test is perfect: some show a problem where none exists, called a false positive. False positives may lead to worry and unnecessary follow-up procedures. For some conditions, doctors debate at which age screening should begin, because the benefits must be weighed against these harms. Patients should discuss their own risk factors before deciding. Guidelines differ between countries. Health services usually send an information leaflet with invitations to screening so that people can consider the potential benefits and drawbacks in advance.
quests.question: A screening test can sometimes suggest a disease that is not actually there.
quests.hint: What is a false positive?
quests.explanation: A result that shows a problem where none exists.
quests.evidenceLine: However, no test is perfect: some show a problem where none exists, called a false positive.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: The idea that we use only ten percent of our brains is a popular myth. Brain scans show activity throughout the brain over the course of a day, and damage to almost any region has some effect. Different tasks activate different areas, which may have created the false impression that most regions are idle. Evolution is also unlikely to have favored an organ that consumes about a fifth of the body's energy but is mostly unused. The myth persists partly because it is encouraging: it suggests hidden potential. Neuroscientists find it hard to correct. Teachers often use the myth as a starting point for lessons on how to evaluate popular claims about science, since it is easy to test.
quests.question: Damage to nearly any region of the brain has some effect.
quests.hint: Read what damage to a brain region does.
quests.explanation: Damage to almost any region has some effect, so no large part is idle.
quests.evidenceLine: Brain scans show activity throughout the brain over the course of a day, and damage to almost any region has some effect.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: A restaurant owner noticed that customers often ordered the cheapest wine on the list. She replaced it with a slightly more expensive bottle and added a very expensive one at the top. Sales of the mid-priced wine rose, because it now looked like a sensible middle choice. The expensive bottle was rarely ordered, but it served its purpose by changing how the other prices seemed. She discovered that adding an option could change decisions without changing what customers wanted. Profit rose noticeably. Restaurant consultants say that many businesses use this effect, and they encourage customers to look at a menu carefully before deciding what they want.
quests.question: The very expensive bottle was the wine customers ordered most.
quests.hint: How often was the expensive bottle ordered?
quests.explanation: It was rarely ordered.
quests.evidenceLine: The expensive bottle was rarely ordered, but it served its purpose by changing how the other prices seemed.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Meetings are often criticized as a waste of time, but the problem is usually their design rather than their existence. A meeting without an agenda tends to wander, and one with too many participants leaves most of them silent. Companies that require every meeting to have a stated purpose and a maximum length report shorter and more useful discussions. Some also insist that decisions and responsibilities be recorded at the end. Attendees say they feel more respected. The change costs nothing. Researchers who study workplaces have proposed simple templates for agendas and summaries that can be printed and used at the start of any meeting.
quests.question: The passage suggests that meetings are worthless in themselves.
quests.hint: Where does the passage locate the problem with meetings?
quests.explanation: It says the problem is usually their design rather than their existence.
quests.evidenceLine: Meetings are often criticized as a waste of time, but the problem is usually their design rather than their existence.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: When people receive a bonus, they often treat it differently from their regular salary. They may spend it on treats, even though the same amount would be carefully budgeted if it were part of monthly income. Economists call this mental accounting: the habit of treating money differently depending on where it came from. Money is identical whatever its origin, so this behavior is not entirely rational. Yet it can be useful, since separating funds helps some people save for specific goals. Rules of thumb do not always need to be logical to work. Financial educators suggest using the habit deliberately, for instance by putting unexpected money into a separate account before it can be spent on impulse.
quests.question: Economists regard mental accounting as a perfectly rational way to handle money.
quests.hint: What do economists say about the logic of this behavior?
quests.explanation: They say the behavior is not entirely rational, since money is identical whatever its origin.
quests.evidenceLine: Money is identical whatever its origin, so this behavior is not entirely rational.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Autocomplete tools on phones predict the next word by analyzing vast collections of text. They are helpful, but they can also nudge writers toward common phrases and away from unusual ones. A study found that people who used predictions wrote messages that were shorter and more similar to one another. Some writers deliberately turn the feature off when they want their own voice to come through. Developers are experimenting with suggestions that offer several different options. The influence is subtle but real. Linguists are also interested in the phenomenon, since it may show how technology slowly changes the way people write and speak to one another.
quests.question: Predictive text can make people's messages more alike.
quests.hint: What did the study find about messages written with predictions?
quests.explanation: They were shorter and more similar to one another.
quests.evidenceLine: A study found that people who used predictions wrote messages that were shorter and more similar to one another.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: The idea that a calorie is a calorie, regardless of its source, is simple but incomplete. A calorie measures the energy released when food burns, and the body does use it as energy. Foods, however, differ in how filling they are, how much energy the body spends digesting them, and how they affect blood sugar. Two hundred calories of nuts tend to satisfy hunger longer than two hundred calories of sweets. Nutritionists therefore focus on the quality of food as well as the quantity. Counting alone can be misleading. Health guidelines in many countries now describe healthy patterns of eating rather than lists of forbidden foods or fixed calorie limits for everyone.
quests.question: The source of calories makes no difference to how full people feel.
quests.hint: Compare two hundred calories of nuts with two hundred of sweets.
quests.explanation: Nuts tend to satisfy hunger longer, so the source does matter.
quests.evidenceLine: Foods, however, differ in how filling they are, how much energy the body spends digesting them, and how they affect blood sugar. Two hundred calories of nuts tend to satisfy hunger longer than two hundred calories of sweets.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Whales sing songs that can last for hours and travel for hundreds of kilometers underwater. Male humpbacks in a region tend to sing the same song at a given time, and the song gradually changes from year to year. Occasionally, a new song spreads rapidly across an ocean, being adopted by whales thousands of kilometers apart. Scientists do not yet know exactly why the songs change, or what information they carry. Some suggest they may be a form of display to attract mates. Others emphasize that the evidence is limited. Recordings made over several decades allow researchers to follow how a single song changes, and they are stored in archives that are open to scientists.
quests.question: The purpose of humpback songs remains uncertain.
quests.hint: Look at what scientists do not yet know.
quests.explanation: They do not know exactly why the songs change or what information they carry.
quests.evidenceLine: Scientists do not yet know exactly why the songs change, or what information they carry.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: A basketball player who scores several shots in a row is often described as having a hot hand. Fans and players firmly believe that success makes the next shot more likely. Early statistical studies found no evidence of this and concluded that the pattern was an illusion of randomness. More recent analyses, using better methods, have detected a small effect in some circumstances. The debate is therefore not entirely settled. Coaches continue to trust their instincts. Some researchers believe that the answer may differ between sports, since basketball, baseball, and volleyball each involve different kinds of repeated attempts.
quests.question: Statistical studies have consistently found strong support for the hot hand.
quests.hint: What did the early studies conclude?
quests.explanation: They found no evidence and called it an illusion, so support was not consistent.
quests.evidenceLine: Early statistical studies found no evidence of this and concluded that the pattern was an illusion of randomness.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: A single unusual storm cannot show whether the climate is changing, since storms have always occurred. Scientists instead look at how the frequency and intensity of events change over decades. In some regions, heavy rainfall has become more common, while in others droughts have become longer. Attribution studies estimate how much a specific event was made more likely by warming, and the answers are usually stated as probabilities. Such results are often summarized in the media as simple yes or no answers. The reality is a matter of degree. Reporters who cover science often say that explaining probabilities to a general audience is one of the hardest parts of their job.
quests.question: Attribution studies usually give simple yes or no answers.
quests.hint: In what form are attribution study answers usually stated?
quests.explanation: As probabilities, while the media simplify them into yes or no.
quests.evidenceLine: Attribution studies estimate how much a specific event was made more likely by warming, and the answers are usually stated as probabilities.

quests.instruction: Read the passage carefully. Based only on what it says, decide whether the statement is true or false.
quests.passage: Students are often told to reread their notes many times before an exam, but this is one of the least effective ways to study. It creates a feeling of familiarity that is mistaken for understanding. Testing yourself, by trying to recall information without looking, strengthens memory more. Spacing study sessions over several days also works better than cramming everything into one night. Teachers who introduce these methods report better results. Many students still prefer the familiar routine. Universities now offer short workshops at the beginning of the year to teach new students these methods before their first examinations.
quests.question: Rereading notes strengthens memory more than testing yourself does.
quests.hint: Compare rereading with self-testing.
quests.explanation: Testing yourself strengthens memory more, not rereading.
quests.evidenceLine: Testing yourself, by trying to recall information without looking, strengthens memory more.
